opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should be careful with the word "simple." I don't think it's easy, and I'm not a biologist, so take this with appropriate salt. What I mean is something more like: it's simple *relative to how hard people intuitively assume it is*, and relative to some of the other problems I spend my time on.

When you compare ageing to something like AI alignment, the target is much clearer. With alignment, part of the difficulty is that we don't fully know what we're aiming for. What does it mean for a system to be honest, or to act in our interests, when it might understand the situation better than we do? There's real conceptual confusion in the problem statement itself. With ageing, the goal is pretty well specified: keep the body functioning roughly the way it does at 25. We have a working example of the thing we want. Every young person is an existence proof.

And nature gives us further hints. There's enormous variation in lifespan across species, sometimes between closely related animals, which suggests the rate of ageing isn't some fixed law of physics. It's tunable. Evolution just hasn't had much reason to optimise for keeping organisms going long after reproduction, so it hasn't.

So the shape of the problem is more like a very large, messy engineering and science problem. Lots of separate damage mechanisms, lots of interacting systems, a lot of work. But it's the kind of thing where you can measure progress, run experiments, and get feedback. That's the sense in which I'd call it relatively tractable. It's hard in a way that more effort and better tools, including AI, can plausibly grind through, rather than hard in a way where we don't even know what success looks like.

Whether that means decades or longer, I genuinely don't know. But I'd be surprised if it turned out to be fundamentally impossible.

r001.rationale: The response describes ageing as a tractable engineering and science problem, but does not identify intervening on ageing’s consequences as an approach that avoids needing a complete understanding of the body’s dynamics.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, "simple" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, so let me be careful about what I mean. I don't think ageing is easy to solve in the sense that we'll have it done next year. What I mean is that it's a relatively well-posed problem compared to a lot of the other big things people worry about.

If you look at something like AI alignment, which is where I spend most of my time, a huge fraction of the difficulty is that we don't even agree on what the problem is. We're not sure what the target is, we're not sure how we'd know if we'd hit it, and the ground keeps moving under us because the systems keep changing. Ageing isn't like that. Ageing is a biological process happening in a physical system that we can measure. We have a very clear success criterion: people stop declining and dying from the accumulated damage of being alive for a long time. You can run experiments, you can get feedback, and the thing you're studying doesn't adapt to your interventions the way an intelligent system does.

The other thing is that there's existence proof that it's not some fundamental law. Different species age at wildly different rates. There are organisms where it's hard to detect any ageing at all. So this isn't like trying to violate thermodynamics. It's an engineering problem where evolution simply never had much incentive to optimise for post-reproductive longevity, and so it didn't. That leaves a lot of room for us to do better than evolution did.

So when I say simple, I mean: the problem is legible, it's bounded, it sits inside physics and chemistry we broadly understand, and the main thing it needs is a lot of careful, well-funded, patient science. That's a very different kind of hard from problems where we're confused about the fundamentals. And honestly, I think it's somewhat underinvested in relative to how clear the payoff is, partly because people have a strong intuition that death is natural and therefore somehow not a thing you're allowed to solve. I just don't find that intuition very compelling.

r001.rationale: The response describes ageing as measurable and amenable to experiments, but does not say that interventions can target its consequences without fully understanding the body's dynamics.

astra-6.text:
I mean “relatively simple” compared with something like aligning a system that’s much smarter than we are. I don’t mean that ageing is easy, or that we already know how to solve it.

With ageing, you’re trying to understand and intervene in a biological process. It’s complicated, but it isn’t actively trying to defeat your attempts to understand it. You can run experiments, learn which mechanisms matter, and gradually improve your interventions. And there’s a fairly concrete outcome you’re looking for: people staying healthy for longer.

With alignment, part of the difficulty is that the system you’re studying might understand the experiment, understand what you want to see, and behave differently when you’re no longer testing it. So the ordinary process of getting reassuring experimental results doesn’t necessarily give you the assurance you need. That’s the sense in which I’d call ageing the relatively simple problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes experimenting on biological mechanisms and improving interventions, but it does not clearly say that intervening on ageing’s consequences can work without fully understanding the body’s dynamics.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean “simple” in a relative sense. Ageing is enormously complicated biologically, but we have an existence proof that biology can build and maintain a human body. The question is how to keep that maintenance working, or repair the damage when it doesn’t.

And you can run experiments, measure what happens, and iterate. That doesn’t make it easy, and I wouldn’t claim we know how to solve it. But it looks like a problem where, with sufficiently good scientific tools, you can make progress through ordinary empirical research. I think that’s a much more favourable situation than a problem where we don’t even know how to tell whether a proposed solution works.

r001.rationale: The response describes maintaining or repairing the body and making empirical progress, but it does not clearly say that these interventions can work without a complete understanding of the body's dynamics.
